title: The Great Depression

cards.h: The crash did not cause it alone, but it lit the match
cards.b:
On Tuesday 29 October 1929, panicked investors dumped 16 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange. Prices crashed.

Within four years, a quarter of American workers had no job, and the whole world was in trouble.
Thousands of US banks failed in the early 1930s, and there was no deposit insurance. World trade shrank by about two thirds.

Governments cut spending and raised tariffs. The US Smoot-Hawley Tariff (1930) set high import taxes, and other countries retaliated. Staying on the gold standard forced many countries into deflation.

By 1933 US unemployment was about 25 percent, and in Germany about 6 million were jobless.

In 1933 Franklin D. Roosevelt took office and began the New Deal: bank rescue, public works, Social Security (1935). John Maynard Keynes's General Theory (1936) argued that governments should spend to revive demand in a slump.

Historians still argue how much the New Deal did; the real recovery came with war spending.

Hardship fed anger. In Germany the Nazis rose from a small party to the largest in 1932. In Japan, the military gained power. The Depression did not make World War II certain, but it made it much likelier.

Myth: after the crash, ruined brokers leapt from skyscrapers by the dozen.Fact: it makes a dramatic story, but records show very few suicides in those weeks. Also, the crash itself did not cause the Depression: weak banks, debt and bad policy turned a crash into a catastrophe.

Five things to remember

  1. The 1929 crash began the slump.
  2. Bank failures and falling trade made it a global depression.
  3. Wrong policies worsened it.
  4. The New Deal and Keynes changed economic thinking.
  5. Hardship helped extremists rise.

Think about it

  • Should governments spend more in a slump?
  • Why did the Depression hit farmers in India?
